event.name: UFC 330
event.notes: Discovery pulls recent uploads from each capper channel and keeps the ones whose title matches settings.discovery.title_contains. Add entries to "videos" only to pin a specific video by hand.

comments.comment: Fading the aging veteran: Ribovics is 10 years younger, more durable and packs more power; used as the third leg of the locky trinity (+101).
Barboza's chin is gone and he's on the back nine; Ribovics is younger, cleaner and well-rounded, though he doubts the big finish so he won't pay the DFS price.
Barboza has the skills but is 40 years old; Ribovics is a good enough striker to find the chin of Barboza.
Ribovics throws huge volume (up to 400 strikes) against an old, retiring Barboza, but the price isn't slam-worthy so only a chalk parlay leg.
Named his most confident pick of the card: Barboza looks washed on a three-fight skid with accumulated damage, and Ribovics' volume and iron chin will drown him.
Parlay leg on the moneyline rather than prop hunting, since Barboza's recent fights other than the Turner loss went to decision and Ribovics may not find the KO.
He's 'kind of just feeling Ribovics' because Barboza, while sharper and more versatile, isn't there physically or health-wise.
Stated as his main card pick to defeat Barboza.
Barboza is on a three-fight losing skid and Ribovics's forward pressure and gunslinging boxing will be too much.
Ribovics is younger, bigger and will pressure with volume; Barboza has been chinned in several recent fights and Ribovics has enough power to break him down.
Both are grappling-heavy but Orolbai has the better gas tank, striking and scrambling to wear Wells down, finishing him in round two or three.
Calls him one of the few guaranteed wins on the card — better wrestler, durable, good jiu-jitsu, and Wells can't get takedowns or win anywhere.
He hasn't bet yet but plans to wait for full markets and play the Orolbai side, citing Orolbai's traits and upside.
Sees it as a bit of a mismatch: Orolbai is sharper and more dangerous on the feet, and unless Wells gets an early finish Orolbai wins nine times out of ten.
Says Orolbai is simply better everywhere — wrestling, striking, chin and cardio — and Wells will fade after the first round.
Said Orolbai wins by any means necessary, any way he wants, with no hesitation ('there's the deep dive').
Orolbai should find the takedowns and keep Wells down; Wells is a striker with lacking takedown defense, making it a bad stylistic matchup.
Included as a leg in his +400 parlay; he expects Alvarez to continue his finishing ways.
Alvarez is the better and far more dangerous fighter everywhere, and Njokuani is gunshy, doesn't wrestle, and has a touch of quit and has been finished.

Leg of his most confident play (2-pick parlay at +104): Alvarez is on another level, better striking dynamism and power plus a big grappling/submission edge over the kickboxer Njokuani, whose losses came against elite fighters.
Already bet Alvarez at 2-to-1; he has huge upside on the ground and with standing guillotines, is more durable, and Njokuani has always been vulnerable grappling.
Taking the short-notice fight signals Alvarez is healthy and was in camp, and he's the better, bigger striker with lightweight skill while Njokuani consistently underwhelms.
One of his strong favorites on the card and a leg of his confident-picks parlay.
Slight lean to Alvarez because his ground game is better; striking is close but the grappling should be the deciding factor.
Ribovics is ten years younger and closer to his prime, landing the bigger shots and countering Barboza's Muay Thai for a knockout.
Expects Ribovics to get right in Barboza's face with combinations and get a late first or early second round finish or mercy stoppage.
Barboza is 40 and has absorbed massive damage recently; Ribovics is durable, high-volume and pressuring, so he expects a punches-in-bunches breakdown finish.
Barboza's striking will shine at times, but Ribovics' pace and constant forward pressure should swing momentum and create the bigger shots.
Barboza is a longtime favorite of Adam's but his chin is completely gone; Adam calls it an easy pick for a quick, brutal first-round knockout.
Barboza is past his prime with a damaged chin and looked bad at weigh-ins; expects Ribovics to knock him out in round one or two.
Barboza at 40 on a three-fight skid can't handle pressure anymore; Ribovics is durable and overwhelming with forward pressure boxing and should land a big shot late.
Barboza is too old and has taken too much damage, and Ribovics gets a pure striking matchup with no takedown threat, so he should knock him out early in round one or two.
Ribovics' pressure, volume and power should overwhelm a 40-year-old Barboza who has taken a lot of damage; no specific round given since it could come in any of the three.
Expects the win to come most likely by KO.
Barboza is old and declining while Ribovics is closer to his prime with pressure and volume; unsure about paying -540.

Colby calls the Ribovics KO possibly his lock of the night; Barboza is 40, on a three-fight skid and was just knocked out, while Ribovics has the finishing upside, leg kicks and pressure to back him into the cage early.
Ribovics closes distance and takes away Barboza's kicking game; Barboza gets rocked and damaged in every fight now, so expects a round one TKO.
Expects the volume and kicks to wear Barboza down for a TKO by the end of round two.
He expects Ribovics to walk Barboza down, cut off the cage and touch his chin for a relatively easy knockout.

Both cappers pick Mansur: Angelo cites a giant grappling gap plus powerful hands and desperation after his TKO loss, while Jacob thinks the striking edge is the difference since Stoltzfus is stationary and hittable.
Perfect bounce-back spot; his athleticism and power should shine through for an early, easy finish. Used in the locky two-step, trinity and +400 parlay.
Abdul-Malik has power, wrestling and is more explosive and athletic than the durable Stoltzfus.
He hasn't bet it yet but says he's probably going to at four-to-one odds, seeing it as a tough physical/athletic matchup for Stoltzfus.
Athletic freak with reach and better wrestling against a middle-of-the-road middleweight; expects him to take Stoltzfus down and smash him early despite the high price.
Favorite lock of the card - a bad stylistic matchup for Stoltzfus, with Abdul Malik the more technical and far bigger puncher.
Abdul-Malik is far better on the feet and Stoltzfus's striking is unimpressive; should be an easy win.
Says he isn't super confident but Abdul-Malik is younger, more physical, with height, reach and power advantages over a hittable Stoltzfus.
Even though he thinks Abdul-Malik is a bottom-feeder middleweight, he's a fast athlete with power and decent takedown defense against a slow, chinnable Stoltzfus.

Lock of the night: Dern is the better BJJ specialist, doesn't let opponents settle on top, creates scrambles and reversals, and has a slight striking edge, while Robertson's submission-over-position style will get her in trouble.
He believes Dern is the better grappler, better wrestler somehow, clearly the better striker and all-time tough; best odds on a confident favorite on the card, so he parlayed her with Abdul-Malik.
Thinks Dern dominates the grappling exchanges and gets it done.
Dern's hands have come a long way so he likes her on the feet, and her elite jiu-jitsu means she'll be fine on the ground against the wrestling of Robertson.
Nick calls it a nightmare matchup for Robertson, saying Dern is better everywhere, has the striking and durability edge and could even land takedowns of her own.
Likes the Dern line as just, considering her the faster, harder striker and the better grappler in a bad stylistic matchup for Robertson, but admits he hasn't placed the bet because he's scared.
Used as a parlay of the week leg: Dern is better everywhere, faster and sharper striking, and will win the grappling exchanges even off her back.

Leg one of the Slam of the Week: he thinks Dern is simply the better fighter, will sweep Robertson off top position and dominate with world-class jiu-jitsu, plus she's hungry as new champion and won't want to lose the belt.

Second leg of the +104 parlay: Dern is better everywhere — powerful pressure striking and world-class jiu-jitsu even off her back — and he's unimpressed with Robertson's recent wins; line dropping toward -200 offers value.
Surprised the price is only -205; thinks Dern is the better striker, grappler and has better five-round cardio, winning scrambles as Robertson gases.
Picks Dern in the co-main event.
States he is very confident: Robertson won't out-grapple or submit Dern, her striking is non-existent, and Dern is the far more physical, aggressive striker who should win nine times out of ten.

picks.selection: Mansur Abdul-Malik by KO/TKO in round 1 or 2

comments.comment: Stoltzfus falls into the category of fighters Abdul-Malik can bang with, find the big shot and knock out as he jumps back into the win column.
Abdul-Malik has too many physical advantages; unless Stoltzfus consistently controls the grappling, Abdul-Malik lands the cleaner, more damaging shots.
Called it the easiest win on the card: Abdul-Malik's D1 wrestling, strong double leg and power are kryptonite to Stoltzfus's back-foot kicking style and fence-hugging.
Expects a TKO on the ground as Abdul-Malik returns to his D1 wrestling roots after a loss, and Stoltzfus has no chin and is very finishable.
Abdul-Malik's power and brutal ground and pound against Stoltzfus' bad chin, poor striking defense and poor takedown defense should equal a knockout.
Thinks Stoltzfus is likely to just go out and lose by KO; used as a leg in his cycle parlay.
Colby doesn't rate Stoltzfus at all (he's been knocked out by Bruno Ferreira) and is very confident Abdul-Malik comes out hot and finds an early, likely first-round KO.
Stoltzfus is chinny and there to be chinned; Abdul-Malik has the athleticism/power edge and finishes cleanly once he hurts someone.
Believes he's too fast on the feet and should score a KO/TKO in the first or second round.

picks.selection: Jalin Turner by KO/TKO in round 1

comments.comment: Turner's speed, power and range, maybe countering a calf kick, leads to a knockout.
Medium confidence: Turner is a gifted, huge, hard-hitting lightweight and Fernandes' opposition wouldn't beat him; a naked leg kick could get him cracked early.
Turner should have the cleaner early moments, punish Fernandez's entries with straight shots and knees, and eventually his size and power make the difference.
Believes Turner finishes it early, before his cardio issues matter, with a first-round knockout.
Fernandez fighting long range at 5'9 against a 6'3 sharp Muay Thai striker is an uphill battle; Turner picks him apart and lands a high kick or hook late.
Turner is the side whenever he faces a non-wrestler, he's enormous for 155, his fights rarely leave round one, and the odds are close.
Leaning on Turner's explosiveness, size and much better level of competition, but calls him untrustworthy mentally and wouldn't jump on the line yet.
Calls it a 60/40 fight; Turner's aggression, size and clinch elbows/knees should get a finish in the first three minutes, otherwise Fernandes wins.

picks.fight: Ian Machado Garry vs Islam Makhachev

comments.comment: Garry can't close the wrestling gap in a couple years of training; Makhachev's smash wrestling and control should dominate, though he doesn't expect a finish.
It may be more competitive than the odds indicate, but nothing stops Makhachev from getting to his Dagestani wrestling; he wears Garry down and wins on the scorecards.

Expects Makhachev's superior trip/body-lock takedown arsenal (like Shavkat's success late) to control Garry to a 49-46/48-47 decision, though Garry's takedown defense and range make it tougher than the JDM fight.

Calls Makhachev the last remaining lock and the GOAT; says Garry is a pillow puncher who won't knock him out, and Makhachev's grappling strength is something Garry has never faced, so it's just a question of submission or decision.
Despite Garry's length and footwork, Makhachev is a good enough grappler to get him down and control him like he did to Della Maddalena.

He's clearly backing Islam ('we can't lose... let's get the win'), saying the face-off made him more confident because Islam looked noticeably bigger and stronger while Garry looked flimsy, and that once Islam gets him to the ground it's going to be a problem; he laments the -400 price being long.
Garry will have success at range, but over five rounds Makhachev's adaptability and constant grappling threats should take over, and extended top time makes it hard for Garry to recover.
Leg two of the Slam of the Week: calls Makhachev the best fighter in the world, 29-1, still in his prime with undiminished athleticism and a better chin at 170, while Garry can't finish anything.
Picks Makhachev in the main event.
Makhachev's wrestling and pressure are too much; Garry won't stop the takedowns and Makhachev's striking is good enough to hold his own.

He says he's leaning with Makhachev and can't pick against him — underrated boxing, elite defensive striking, and by far the better wrestler/grappler, though he acknowledges a Garry head-kick KO is the main upset path.

picks.selection: Ramiz Brahimaj by submission in round 1

comments.comment: Most of Magny's submission losses come in round one and Brahimaj gets his subs early, so the round-one sub at +450 was preferred over the plain round-one price.
Jacob says he will definitely have action on Brahimaj early — first or second round submission — since Brahimaj chases the guillotine relentlessly and Magny is lazy with his head position.
A lean: Johnson is faster, in great shape, gets in your face throwing bombs, and McConico is slower and less durable and won't want to exchange.
Interested in Johnson's finishing potential; his speed and early aggression should find the opening even if McConico has moments in the clinch.
Considered the McConico underdog but capped his card at three dogs; picks Johnson to KO him because McConico doesn't take damage well and only went to a near-split with Johnson previously.
Likes Johnson's powerful striking and combinations; if he stays patient he'll crack McConico's chin and finish him.
Adam takes Johnson by knockout but says he isn't convinced and wouldn't be shocked if Johnson dropped an ugly decision after his close fight with Brundage.
Johnson's boxing is his real skill set and McConico hates being backed up and hit; the worry is Johnson's terrible fight IQ leading him to wrestle again.
Brody sticks with Johnson's power and youth, distrusting McConico's chin (he's been knocked out before) and following his pattern that a sub win then a decision win is followed by a KO.
Chapelin took the fight on three days' notice so Johnson has the better gas tank and preparation; his boxing and distance work should win him the later rounds on points.
Leans Johnson to get it done most likely by decision, possibly racking up control time with his wrestling; also used as a leg in a subscriber's longshot parlay with Luque by submission.
Johnson is longer, craftier, higher volume and can mix in takedowns, and Chapulin brings no wrestling threat on roughly three days' notice; expects a late TKO or clear decision.
Calls it a borderline pick'em but favors Johnson's UFC experience, height/range and level of competition over Chapelin's power and danger factor.
Tobias lacks output; Fernando is the better striker with power and combinations, and his takedown defense should hold up.
Long, technical, defensively sound striker against a limited grappler; risky as a UFC debutant so he'd fade him in DFS but still picks him to win.
Confident play: Fernando's Muay Thai, low kicks and mixed striking are a level above Tobias, and his takedown defense should keep the fight standing.
Fernando is the bigger, more athletic man with an 80-inch reach, better finishing ability, good low kicks and momentum from two first-round finishes in LFA.

picks.selection: Tresean Gore by submission in round 1

comments.comment: Called it his pick of the week at even money: Luque is finishable and less durable/driven now, while Gore hits hard, has sick submissions and proved himself by finishing Azamat Bekoev.
Leg of his +400 parlay; Turner's speed, power and range should find Fernandes' chin.
Despite liking Fernandes historically, he thinks Turner has far more skills plus knockout power, length and a grappling edge.
George likes Turner's size as a weight bully at lightweight, points to the good bounce-back finish and green flags from the fight-week interview and new contract.
Turner is the far better boxer, one of the best at countering kicks, and should walk Fernandes down and make it a boxing fight; wins by decision or early KO as a slight favorite.
Turner's frame, power and submission threat give him the tools to win as long as his legs don't get chopped up.
Agrees with the odds: Fernandes' leg-kick win came over a short-notice featherweight, and rangy Turner (6'3", 77-inch reach) can catch him on the chin in a real exchange.
Confident play: Turner's big height/reach edge (6'3 vs 5'9) lets him control range and counter Fernandes' kicks with straight shots, and he's live to finish.

Turner is huge for the division, very well-rounded with a great jab and power plus dangerous jiu-jitsu; despite being a little worried about Fernandes' elite leg kicks, he thinks Turner is simply the better fighter and should get it done.
Fernando is the longer, far cleaner striker with good low kicks and knees, while Tobias is flat-footed, hittable and not a good enough wrestler to get the fight down.
Fernando is far faster, more athletic and throws straight down the middle with body work, while Tobias is slow and can't grapple with him.
Admits he hasn't watched Fernando fight, but thought Tobias looked mid in his last outing, so takes Fernando by KO.
Watched him a lot in LFA and calls it a tailor-made spot for a first-round knockout.
Tobias looked awful and not UFC-ready in his debut, so Adam takes Fernando to win by TKO.
Fernando's Pedro Rizzo kickboxing, devastating leg kicks and reach plus strong defensive grappling/wall-walking should outclass Tobias, who won't control him long enough.
Fernando's striking is cleaner and more powerful with a huge reach advantage, while Tobias relies on takedowns that failed against Da'Mon Blackshear; he sees a second or third round finish.
Fernando is a massive LFA double champion with power and better level of competition, and Tobias struggles on the feet and plods around, so he expects a first-round knockout.

Colby thinks Tobias fails against step-ups in competition and is poor on the feet, while Fernando has faced better opposition (Cesar Almeida, Azamat Bekoev), has momentum and a big reach edge, and will pressure him to a likely first-round KO.
Expects the size, power and finishing potential to show up early for a first-round TKO.
He cashed the over in Johnson's last fight and believes it will be fruitful again here.

picks.fight: Ian Machado Garry vs Islam Makhachev

comments.comment: He only needs Garry to win one round (or win the fight outright); Garry's range management, distance and oblique kicks should get him at least a round, and he doesn't expect a JDM-style five-round blanketing.

picks.selection: Joel Alvarez by submission in round 1

comments.comment: Says he'll likely put money down at -200; Njokuani is on a two-fight losing streak and has been finished quickly recently, so Alvarez takes his back or gets an arm triangle early.

picks.selection: Jose Ochoa by KO/TKO in round 2

comments.comment: Johnson gets wobbly when hit clean, was knocked out by Alex Perez and stopped by Asu Almabayev a month ago with little prep time, and Ochoa hits hard.
Sam switched off the over, expecting Ribovics to come out like a madman and finish Barboza early.
Stoltzfus is chinny and they consider the under a great price for an early finish.
Both men are tough and have been in extended fights and decisions; neither is a kill-or-be-killed heavyweight type, so the fight should last past round one.

picks.selection: Mansur Abdul-Malik to win and fight starts round 2

comments.comment: Coming off his first loss, Mansur should be patient early and finish later, while the experienced Stoltzfus is live enough to survive round one (his last two fights went to decision).
Already bet the over to cover his Ochoa-by-decision prediction, trusting Charles Johnson's traits to survive and rally in round three.
Ochoa is the younger, active, intense striker with decent takedown defense; sees it as a passing of the torch over the 36-year-old Johnson.
Angelo slightly leans Ochoa because Charles Johnson takes too long to get going and Ochoa starts fast, but he calls the line disrespectful and won't bet it.
Ochoa is the younger fighter, an explosive and sharp striker who can also grapple a bit.
Johnson is washed with a shaky chin while Ochoa is younger, quicker, hungrier and more powerful.
Picks Ochoa to beat Johnson in the featured fight.
He believes Abdul-Malik runs through Stoltzfus and knocks him out in the first round.
Great price only because Abdul-Malik has underperformed before; against a chinny Stoltzfus he should knock him out in the first if he's serious about his career.
He expects Abdul-Malik to dominate and find an early finish, probably first round.
Part of his inside-the-distance parlay because both fighters in the pairing are big finishers.
Since he's picking Brahimaj and Brahimaj is submission-or-bust, the finish should come early.
Sam expects a finish either way given Luque's durability questions and Gore's power/guillotine, so the under is a fine alternative to a side.

picks.selection: Myktybek Orolbai by submission in round 1

comments.comment: He sees it ending early with Orolbai getting him down and wrapping up a submission, probably in the first round.

picks.selection: Jose Ochoa by KO/TKO in round 2

comments.comment: He expects Ochoa to just throw hands and knock Johnson out early, in the first or second round, rather than go for a submission.
Ochoa's rare power at 125 will get Johnson's respect, Johnson is coming off a bad KO loss and fighting too often, and he won't offensively wrestle Ochoa.
Expects the win most likely by KO.
Vowed never to pick Johnson again; Johnson is hittable to the left hook and starts slow, while Ochoa has crisp boxing and in his view beat Alibayev.
Leans Ochoa: aggressive southpaw with power who will put the declining, recently-finished Johnson on the back foot and land the left hand on his open right side.
He thinks Alvarez adds an 18th submission win to his record.
A lean toward Alvarez getting wild, closing distance into the pocket and finishing, though he admits Njokuani is a live underdog with more betting value.
Adam argues the fight ends up on the mat somehow (knockdown, slip, failed kick) and Alvarez's 19 career submissions give him a massive ground edge; Sam said he's down for both.
If Alvarez can get past Njokuani's striking and force grappling exchanges, his submission game from unusual positions eventually takes over.
Alvarez's grappling is far superior and Njokuani's takedown defense and grappling are weak.
Njokuani's high narrow stance is wide open to takedowns and he's a fish out of water on the ground against Alvarez's elite chokes; the usual length advantage is negated by Alvarez's size.
Alvarez is better everywhere and has only lost to elite fighters while Njokuani just lost to Carlos Leal; one takedown and the fight is over, and the submission price offers plus money.
Njokuani is a striker who struggles badly once the fight hits the mat and has a poor get-up game, while Alvarez is a prolific early submission finisher.
Colby thinks Alvarez is better everywhere, is younger, and has nine or ten first-round subs; Njokuani was just submitted in the first round by a lesser grappler in Jake Matthews.
Floats that Alvarez may even get the finish by submission.
Njokuani has been submitted recently (Jake Matthews) and Alvarez should blitz then find takedowns into a submission.
Surprised by the money on Robertson; he doesn't see her out-grappling Dern, and Robertson taking chances leaves an opening for Dern to slap on a submission.
Robertson will be confident enough to engage in the grappling and advance position, which he thinks gets her submitted.
Robertson failed takedowns and got reversed against Lipski; against Dern those same transitions lead to a submission.
Dern is better everywhere — grappling, speed, power, experience — with only size favoring Robertson; she stuns her standing and shows a new level of grappling.
Dern has the striking edge and Robertson's grappling will put her in submission danger; leaning Dern but waiting on weigh-ins and face-offs.
Robertson lacks the power to hurt Dern on the feet and will shoot takedowns into Dern's elite jiu-jitsu; expects an armbar.
Colby thinks Dern is bigger, stronger, the better grappler and has better hands, and that Robertson only needs one mistake on the mat; he takes Dern by submission around round three.

picks.selection: Myktybek Orolbai by submission in round 1

comments.comment: Says Orolbai will smoke and submit Wells, pointing to Wells getting put to sleep by Carlston Harris and being folded up in round one.
Calls it the easiest pick on the card: Orolbai is far better on the ground, has wins over ranked opposition, and Wells will get taken down and submitted or rocked into a panic takedown into a d'arce.

Wells is 39 and on the back end of his career while Orolbai has insane wrestling and power; they expect a quick takedown and submission, likely in round one (Wells has never been KO'd, so submission over KO).
Thinks Orolbai will hunt a finish this time after going to decision last time out, and gets it via chain wrestling into a submission.
Expects Fernando to outlast and chop down the 23-year-old Tobias with diverse striking, so he'll reach for the round two and three finish props rather than the short moneyline price.
Fernando has a 7-inch reach and height edge, wins on the feet, and Tobias has been knocked out before and didn't look great in his debut.
He feels Fernando can find a finish, calling it a second-round finish.

picks.selection: Ramiz Brahimaj by submission in round 1

comments.comment: 12 of Brahimaj's 13 wins are submissions, mostly in round one, and if he beats Magny it is far and away by submission, so he plans to play that prop.
Magny's submission defense is his glaring weakness and Brahimaj is a submission hunter, so the layer-cake includes the straight sub prop.
Brahimaj is faster, stronger, more powerful with crushing submissions and better takedowns, a horrible stylistic matchup for a past-prime Magny who can't defend leg kicks or takedowns.
The fight only goes two ways: Brahimaj by submission or Magny by decision, so take the juiced submission payout instead of the moneyline.
Brahimaj only wins by submission and usually in round one, and Magny has always struggled with submission defense; the fight is either a Brahimaj finish or a Magny decision.
Magny is 39 and has been caught in chokes in his recent fights, while Brahimaj is a strong submission artist who should find Magny's neck.

Brody won't bet on old fighters; he sees Brahimaj coming out fast with improved hands, getting to the hips and finding a first-round submission since Magny struggles with grapplers and Brahimaj has 10 first-round subs.
Plus money prop: Brahimaj is a high-level grappler with 12 submission wins and Magny is aging against a younger, hungrier fighter.

picks.fight: Ian Machado Garry vs Islam Makhachev
picks.selection: Islam Makhachev by submission in round 3

comments.comment: Doesn't rate Garry's stand-up; expects Makhachev to get takedowns and cage control like the Shavkat fight and hunt a finish (darce choke) after his flat JDM performance.
He thinks Garry survives to the third but gets taken down and choked out, so submission in round 3.
Turner is a huge, powerful lightweight now training at Bloodline MMA and typically doesn't win when the fight leaves round one, so the round 1 price is nearly the same as his moneyline.
He suggests the round 1 prop because it could come as a knockout, a club-and-sub, or a submission off a back take — he expects Turner to get it done early.
He expects Turner to come out like a madman, pin Fernandes on the cage and finish him early; if it gets past round one Fernandes becomes live.
Adam can't trust Luque after 37 pro fights, a brain injury and multiple finish losses, and Gore hits hard with a strong guillotine, though he admits he isn't confident.
Doesn't like Luque's move up to 185 at age 35 after recent poor showings, while Gore is the bigger man and dangerous with front chokes.
Gore has a solid chin, is a scrapper coming off a good KO win, and Luque won't just clip him with a check hook.
Jacob takes the dog Magny as the safer pick, saying it's a tailor-made Magny fight where he weathers the early submission threat and wears Brahimaj down for the decision.
Fading Brahimaj, who he doesn't believe is UFC level; thinks Magny is the better striker with better takedown defense and cardio.
Thinks Brahimaj is overrated with wins only over cans, while Magny has huge height/reach, experience and a grappling edge and can pick him apart off the back foot for a decision.
Doesn't think Brahimaj has any top-level wins or the power to finish Magny, and expects Magny to clinch him up against the cage and control him on top; odds are close.
Colby leans Magny as a legit gatekeeper who is the more skilled fighter and doesn't think Brahimaj is on the level of the guys Magny has lost to.
Considered McConico as the more well-rounded fighter but thinks Johnson's pace, pressure and power striking dictates the fight and wins on the scorecards.
Johnson is faster, more athletic and hits harder, while McConico has been knocked out in both UFC losses.
Close fight but McConico gets rocked once opponents find his chin; Johnson's power, ground and pound and move to Extreme Couture win it by decision or KO.
Leg of the -118 three-pick parlay: Johnson is more athletic, powerful and youthful, McConico's losses come by knockout, and Johnson has a new Vegas camp sparring with Sean Strickland.

picks.fight: Ian Machado Garry vs Islam Makhachev
picks.selection: Islam Makhachev by submission in round 4

comments.comment: They believe if Makhachev finishes it's by submission (arm triangle), likely within three rounds, since Garry is ineffective off his back.
He sees Islam having a field day controlling Garry on his back and finishing him thanks to Garry's long limbs and long neck, calling submission a very high probability.
Makhachev's elite sambo/judo grappling, improving striking and IQ, plus reportedly 11 lbs of added muscle making him heavier than Garry on fight night, means Garry is in trouble once grabbed.
Nobody defends Makhachev's takedowns and Garry lacks one-punch power, so Garry would have to win a decision; Makhachev drags him late for a finish.
Despite giving Garry a 35-40% chance and outlining a game plan for him, he still picks Islam by submission, believing Islam should be able to secure takedowns and control time.

Makhachev has solved every advantage Garry has before (size, reach, boxing), is elite in scrambles with the d'arce and back takes, and Garry can't finish him or out-decision him with Khabib game-planning.

They don't see Garry surviving 25 minutes; Makhachev will get it to the ground, wear him out with his weight and find the sub later in the fight (rounds three through five), with Garry also seen as distracted.

picks.selection: Dante Johnson by KO/TKO in round 2

comments.comment: Adam likes covering both rounds for the knockout and both hosts placed the round-two KO alongside the round-one.
Johnson has never lost as a pro, bangs on the feet and gets takedowns with good ground and pound, while McConico has been seen to break as fights go on.

picks.selection: Esteban Ribovics by KO in round 1

comments.comment: He expects Ribovics to get it done early, knocking Barboza out within a round and a half.
40-year-old Barboza is on a three-fight losing streak and will shell up as Ribovics lands more and more before finishing him early.

picks.selection: Gillian Robertson by submission in round 2

comments.comment: Going with his gut on an upset: Dern feels like she could lose any fight, and Robertson is on a long win streak with great reversals and submissions from the bottom; armbar finish.

picks.fight: Ian Machado Garry vs Islam Makhachev
picks.selection: Fight does not go the distance

comments.comment: Jacob wanted Islam inside the distance at +150 but took fight doesn't go the distance at +120 to also cover a weird Garry finish; he expects Islam to wear Garry down and submit him.
Colby expects Orolbai to finish quickly and easily, so he's taking the under on what he assumes will be a 1.5-round line.
Luque is the technically superior fighter and, as long as his durability holds, should counter Gore and find a clinch/submission opportunity.
Luque has fought far better competition and just beat Kelvin Gastelum; his jiu-jitsu is levels above Gore's, so once he gets a takedown it's a wrap.
